chapter_theme: An unnamed First One, known only through epithets, is made the ground of learning, freedom from anxiety and the crossing of the sea. The chapter's recurring claim is exclusive: without reaching those feet, these things are out of reach.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the First One's existence (1), learning's fruit (2), those who think of, praise and follow him reach release (3-6), the fault of not doing so (7-9), and both outcomes stated together (10).

1.reading: As all letters have 'a' as their first, the world has the Primal Lord as its first.
1.nuance: The verse gives a simile of being first and says nothing of creating. Parimelazhagar reads it as establishing that the unseen deity exists, arguing from the visible world, which is more than the couplet states.

2.reading: What has learning achieved if the learned do not bow at the good feet of the one of pure knowledge?
2.nuance: The question assumes that learning has a purpose beyond itself. It is the chapter's first conditional, and it is put to the learned, not to the ignorant.

positions.position: The one of pure knowledge is God, and scriptural knowledge bears fruit by worship that cuts off rebirth.
positions.quote: ஆகம அறிவிற்குப் பயன் அவன் தாளைத் தொழுது பிறவியறுத்தல்

positions.position: The one meant is any person greater in knowledge, and the failing is a lack of humility before such people.
positions.quote: தன்னைவிட அறிவில் மூத்த பெருந்தகையாளரின் முன்னே வணங்கிநிற்கும் பண்பு

3.reading: Those who reach the noble feet of the one who walked upon the flower will live long upon the earth.
3.nuance: The Tamil says நிலமிசை, on the earth, so reading it as a world above is an interpretation. Parimelazhagar also rejects an identification of 'the one who walked on the flower' with another deity, which shows the epithet was already disputed.

positions.position: The long life is deathless life in the world of release, above all worlds.
positions.quote: எல்லா உலகிற்கும் மேலாய் வீட்டு உலகின்கண் அழிவின்றி வாழ்வார்

positions.position: The general word 'land' covers this world and the next, with enjoyment named before release.
The long life is the lasting renown of those who follow such a person.

4.reading: Those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering, anywhere or at any time.
4.nuance: The one sought is defined by what he lacks. Parimelazhagar's explanation makes the benefit mimetic: those who reach him also lose liking and aversion, and so lose the suffering these cause.

positions.position: The suffering removed is that of rebirth, in its three classical kinds.
The one meant is a selfless human example, and following such a person keeps ordinary suffering away.
positions.quote: விருப்பு வெறுப்பற்றுத் தன்னலமின்றித் திகழ்கின்றவரைப் பின்பற்றி நடப்பவர்களுக்கு

5.reading: The two kinds of deed born of darkness do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
5.nuance: The verse says both kinds, so good deeds are also among what must not cling. That is a stronger claim than 'worship removes sin'.

positions.position: Even good deeds cause birth, and the praise is true only of the one who has all divine qualities.
Those who understand what 'the Lord' means and seek renown meet good and bad with equal measure.
positions.quote: நன்மை தீமைகளை ஒரே அளவில் எதிர் கொள்வார்கள்.

6.reading: Those who stand firm on the truthful path of conduct of the one who quenched the five senses' desires will live long.
6.nuance: This is the only verse in the chapter that asks for a way of living instead of reaching or praising. Parimelazhagar says the path was taught by the one who quenched the five, as a poem belongs to its poet, which makes him a teacher and not only an object of worship.

7.reading: Except for those who reach the feet of the incomparable one, it is hard to remove the mind's anxiety.
7.nuance: The verse says அரிது, hard. Parimelazhagar explicitly takes this as impossibility, which hardens the claim beyond its plain wording.

8.reading: Except for those who reach the feet of the gracious one who is a sea of virtue, the other seas are hard to swim.
8.nuance: The sea of virtue set against 'other seas' is the image's whole point. Pope's gloss, 'sea of vice', is not in the Tamil.

positions.position: The other seas are wealth and pleasure, set apart from virtue in the three aims of life.
The அந்தணன் is a worthy human being, whose example carries others across seas of trouble.

9.reading: A head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities is as useless as a sense organ that cannot sense.
9.nuance: The verse never lists the eight. Parimelazhagar gives a list from Saiva scripture and records rival lists, so any particular list is the commentator's. Manakkudavar goes further and says such bodies lack life.

positions.position: The eight qualities are those taught in the Saiva agamas, though others list them differently.

10.reading: Those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births, and those who do not reach them cannot.
10.nuance: The chapter closes with both outcomes in one couplet. Verses 7 and 8 hedge with 'hard', and this one drops the hedge. Parimelazhagar's 'reach' comes from the verse's own closing negative, since the positive verb is left implied.

positions.position: The sea is the shoreless chain of cause and effect in rebirth.
positions.quote: காரண காரியத் தொடர்ச்சியாய் கரை இன்றி வருதலின்

positions.position: The sea is life in this world, which is hard to cross without following a leading person.

links.note: The opening verse sets the world under a First One without reservation. In 1062, Valluvar curses whoever ordered the world so that people must beg to live. Read together, they show the book does not treat the world's source as beyond moral judgement.
Here learning has no fruit without bowing at the feet. In 400, learning itself is the one imperishable wealth, with no such condition.
The same word, ஐந்தவித்தான், describes the Lord here and a human renunciant in 25. Sharing the epithet suggests that the divine model and the human achievement are not wholly separate.
Here only those at the Lord's feet cross the sea of births. In 38, on the commentators' reading, a daily good deed blocks the road of births, and God is not mentioned.

source_issues: Manakkudavar's comment on verse 9 ends with a stray '10', apparently a verse or page number.
Parimelazhagar's comment on verse 10 has spelling slips: இரைவன் for இறைவன் and பிரவி for பிறவி.
